blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: The switch adds a destination built on jPOS's Common Message Format. Your terminals speak ISO 8583:1987 over a link packed with iso87ascii.xml. The new destination declines a purchase with action code 1001, and the switch copies that field 39 into the terminal's reply unchanged. What does the terminal receive?

options.text: A reply with 39=1001, since the switch sends field 39 exactly as the destination wrote it
options.says: the reply is packed for the terminal's link, where field 39 holds two characters, so it never leaves

options.text: No reply, since the four-digit code does not fit the link's two-character field 39
options.says: packing fails with 'Field length 4 too long. Max: 2'; SendResponse only notes it in the Context, and the terminal times out

options.text: A reply with 39=54, since the link's packager converts the CMF code into its 1987 equivalent
options.says: a packager packs values and knows nothing of response codes; translating them is the switch's job

options.text: No reply, since the link's packager refuses any code that ISO 8583:1987 does not define
options.says: the packager checks the length of field 39, not its value; a two-character code it doesn't know would pack

origin.section: 16.3 A Destination's Code Becomes a Cause, and Each Source's Table Answers It

questions.stem: Your switch's table for one network lists the codes 00, 05, 51 and 54. That network answers a purchase with 10, which its specification calls a partial approval. What should the switch do?

options.text: Answer the terminal 05 and send nothing upstream, since a code missing from the table counts as a refusal
options.says: an unlisted code may be an approval; taken for a refusal, the network keeps the cardholder's money for a purchase the terminal declined

options.text: Answer the terminal 10 and send nothing upstream, since the code already fits the terminal's two-character field
options.says: the switch never passes a destination's code through; the source's own table decides what the terminal hears

options.text: Answer the terminal 96 and reverse the purchase upstream, since the network may have taken the money
options.says: a code the table lacks leaves the outcome unknown, like silence, so the switch reverses what it sent and answers 96

options.text: Answer the terminal 96 and send the purchase again, since the network may not have understood it
options.says: the page reverses what was sent when the outcome is unknown; it never sends the request again

origin.section: 16.4 A Code the Table Lacks Is Like Silence, and the Switch Reverses What It Sent

questions.stem: In the switch's forwarding group, QueryHost has continuations set to false. The participant after it, which reverses what was sent when no answer came, is a plain participant. A network approves a purchase, and its answer is lost on the way back. What happens?

options.text: The terminal gets 91 and no reversal is queued, since the reversing participant is not asked once QueryHost has failed the transaction
options.says: without continuations QueryHost votes FAIL on a timeout; after an abort only abort participants are asked, so the plain participant never runs

options.text: The terminal gets 91 and a reversal is queued, since the reversing participant still runs after QueryHost on the abort path
options.says: the page says MapResponse never runs once QueryHost has voted FAIL: after an abort a plain participant is not asked

options.text: The terminal gets nothing and a reversal is queued, since without continuations QueryHost holds the session until the terminal gives up
options.says: QueryHost waits its own timeout, then fails the transaction with HOST_UNREACHABLE, which the answering participant turns into 91

options.text: The terminal gets nothing and no reversal is queued, since without continuations QueryHost waits for the answer forever
options.says: the timeout still applies without continuations; the transaction aborts and the terminal gets 91

origin.section: 16.4 A Code the Table Lacks Is Like Silence, and the Switch Reverses What It Sent

questions.stem: To keep fewer records, a developer moves the line that records what was sent upstream from before QueryHost to after it, guarded so that it runs only when HOST_RESPONSE is in the Context. Which purchases can the switch then no longer reverse upstream?

options.text: Purchases the destination declined, since the guard skips a response that carries a decline code
options.says: a decline is a response, so the guarded line still records it

options.text: Purchases that timed out upstream, since the guard skips a response that arrives after the timeout
options.says: after a timeout HOST_RESPONSE is absent, so the moved line records nothing, and neither the switch nor the terminal's reversal finds the purchase

options.text: Purchases the destination approved, since the guard skips a response once the reply has gone out
options.says: the guard runs before any reply is sent, and only a reversal takes the record

options.text: Purchases sent on a second link, since the guard skips a response that came through another QMUX
options.says: every QMUX's answer lands under HOST_RESPONSE the same way; the records are the switch's, keyed by the source's request

origin.section: 16.2 A Source's Reversal Finds What the Destination Saw Only Through the Switch's Record

concepts: A destination's response code is translated into a cause and each source's table turns the cause into its own code; passed through, a code from another format can make the reply unsendable.
A plain participant after QueryHost runs only while the transaction is prepared; with continuations off, a timeout aborts first and nothing reverses the silent purchase.
The record is written before the request leaves, because the purchase that most needs a reversal is the one whose answer never came.
A code the destination's table lacks leaves the outcome unknown, like silence, so the switch reverses what it sent, once, and answers 96 or 91 rather than a decline.
